The password was a reasonable idea in 1961, when Fernando Corbató added one to the Compatible Time-Sharing System at MIT so that researchers could keep their files apart. It is a bad idea in 2026, when the average person maintains more than a hundred accounts and reuses the same handful of strings across most of them.

The alternatives exist. Single sign-on through SSO providers lets a company retire dozens of passwords at once. Passkeys, which Apple, Google, and Microsoft all now support, replace the shared secret with a key pair that never leaves the device. Hardware tokens have protected Google's own employees from phishing since 2017 without a single successful account takeover.

What holds adoption back is not technology but habit, and habit is a product problem. Until the passwordless path is the default on the sign-up screen rather than an option buried in settings, most people will keep typing the name of their first pet.
